Loose Implant Screw: Causes, Symptoms and Treatment Options

Understanding why the screw connecting an implant crown may become loose, how to recognise the signs, and what professional treatment options may be available.

Book Assessment1-Hour Consultation020 71833573

Dental implants are made up of several precisely engineered components that work together to support a functional and natural-looking replacement tooth. The implant fixture is placed within the jawbone, and a small connecting piece called an abutment is secured to the fixture using a specialised screw. The visible crown is then attached to this abutment, completing the restoration.

The abutment screw plays a critical role in maintaining the stability of the implant restoration. In some cases, this screw may loosen over time due to a variety of factors, including bite forces, component wear, or changes in how the teeth come together. Patients may notice slight movement of the crown, a clicking sensation when chewing, or discomfort when biting down.

A loose implant screw does not necessarily mean that the implant itself has failed. In many cases, the implant fixture remains securely integrated within the jawbone, and the issue can be addressed by treating the screw or the connecting components. Professional dental assessment is recommended to determine the cause and identify the most appropriate treatment approach.

What Is a Loose Implant Screw?

A loose implant screw refers to a situation where the small screw that connects the implant crown or abutment to the implant fixture has become unstable. This screw is designed to hold the restoration firmly in place, and when it loosens, the crown or abutment may begin to move or feel insecure.

It is important to distinguish between a loose screw and a failing implant. In many instances, the implant itself remains stable and well-integrated within the jawbone. The movement that patients experience is often confined to the crown or abutment component, rather than the fixture that sits within the bone.

A clinical examination is required to confirm the source of the problem. This may involve checking the implant fixture for stability, inspecting the crown and abutment, and evaluating the condition of the screw itself. Dental imaging may also be used to assess the implant components and surrounding bone structure.

Common Causes of a Loose Implant Screw

Several factors may contribute to an implant screw becoming loose. In many cases, more than one factor may be involved, and a thorough clinical assessment is needed to identify the specific cause.

Bite Pressure or Uneven Bite Alignment

If the implant crown is subjected to excessive or uneven bite forces, the repetitive stress can gradually loosen the abutment screw over time. Changes in the bite following other dental treatments may also alter force distribution across the implant.

Teeth Grinding or Clenching

Bruxism — the habit of grinding or clenching the teeth, often during sleep — can place significant lateral and vertical forces on the implant restoration. Over time, these forces may cause the abutment screw to gradually work loose.

Wear of Implant Components

Like all mechanical components, the screw, abutment, and crown undergo gradual wear through normal daily use. Over many years, this natural wear can reduce the precision of the connection and allow minor movement to develop.

Improper Load Distribution

If the implant restoration does not distribute chewing forces evenly, concentrated stress on specific areas of the screw connection may contribute to loosening. This can sometimes occur if the crown is not precisely aligned with the opposing teeth.

Changes in Bite After Dental Treatment

Following other dental procedures — such as new crowns, bridges, or orthodontic treatment — the way the teeth come together may change. These alterations can modify the forces acting on the implant screw and potentially contribute to loosening.

Screw Fatigue

The abutment screw is subject to repeated mechanical loading with every bite and chewing action. Over extended periods, metal fatigue may develop in the screw, reducing its clamping force and allowing the connection to become less secure.

Signs and Symptoms of a Loose Implant Screw

The signs of a loose implant screw may develop gradually or become apparent suddenly. Patients who notice any of the following should consider seeking professional dental assessment to determine whether the screw requires attention.

Slight movement or wobbling of the implant crown when touched
A clicking or tapping sensation when chewing or biting down
Discomfort or a dull ache when biting on the implant crown
A noticeable change in how the teeth come together when biting
Food becoming trapped around the implant crown more frequently
A feeling that the crown is sitting differently or has shifted slightly
Gum tenderness or mild irritation around the implant restoration
An unusual metallic taste if the screw connection becomes exposed

Symptoms may vary depending on the extent of looseness and which component is affected. Even mild symptoms should be evaluated, as early treatment may help prevent further complications.

Potential Effects on Implant Function

A loose implant screw can affect several aspects of daily oral function if left unaddressed. While the issue is often treatable, seeking timely assessment may help prevent the problem from progressing.

Chewing ability may be reduced, as patients may instinctively avoid using the side of the mouth where the implant is located. This can lead to uneven bite distribution and place additional strain on the remaining natural teeth, potentially contributing to further dental concerns over time.

Crown stability is directly affected by the condition of the abutment screw. A loose screw allows micro-movement of the crown, which can accelerate wear on the screw threads and other connecting components. If the screw becomes severely loose, the crown may eventually detach entirely from the implant.

The long-term integrity of the implant components may also be compromised. Continued movement can cause wear to the internal connection of the implant fixture, and bacteria may enter the gap between the crown and abutment, potentially increasing the risk of inflammation around the implant site. Regular dental implant maintenance can help identify potential issues before they progress.

Treatment Options for a Loose Implant Screw

Treatment for a loose implant screw depends on the clinical findings and the specific cause of the instability. A thorough examination is essential before determining the most appropriate course of action. Options vary depending on the condition of the implant components and may include:

Tightening or Replacing the Abutment Screw

If the screw has loosened but remains in good condition, it can often be re-tightened to the correct torque during a clinical appointment. Where the screw has worn or sustained damage, a replacement screw may be fitted. This may help restore stability to the implant restoration.

Adjusting Bite Forces

If excessive or uneven bite pressure has contributed to the screw loosening, occlusal adjustments may be recommended. These adjustments aim to distribute chewing forces more evenly across the implant and surrounding teeth, reducing the risk of future loosening.

Repair or Replacement of Implant Components

Where the crown, abutment, or other components have worn or sustained damage, repair or implant crown replacement may be recommended. Treatment depends on clinical assessment and the condition of each component, and aims to restore the implant restoration to full function.

Monitoring the Implant Restoration

In some cases, particularly where symptoms are mild and the screw remains partially stable, careful monitoring with regular follow-up appointments may be appropriate. This allows the dental team to track any changes and intervene promptly if the situation progresses.

Importance of Professional Implant Evaluation

Implant restorations should be evaluated by a dental professional if any movement or instability is noticed. Even seemingly minor symptoms may indicate an issue that could benefit from early intervention, potentially helping to avoid more complex or extensive treatment at a later stage.

A thorough examination may involve checking the stability of the implant fixture within the bone, inspecting the condition of the crown and abutment, evaluating the torque and integrity of the abutment screw, and reviewing dental imaging where appropriate. These investigations help determine whether the issue is limited to the screw or whether other components may also be affected.

Assessment and treatment planning for dental implant restorations are available at our London clinic, where professional evaluation can help determine appropriate care options. Where a loose screw is identified, early treatment may help restore stability and support the continued function of the implant restoration.
